content.text: A single-phase 7 kW home charger adds around 37 km of range per hour of charging for most current electric cars. On a standard overnight 8-hour charge from 20 percent. That is around 296 km of range: more than most UK drivers need for a week. The choice of 7 kW versus 22 kW is relevant only if the car battery is very large or if daytime rapid charging is required.

has the cable attached permanently to the unit. You plug the car end into the car and leave the charger end in the unit. It is faster to use each day but less flexible if you change car brand or share the charger with multiple cars of different connector types. An untethered charger has a socket on the unit; you supply your own cable. The cable goes with the car if you sell the charger or move house.

Most UK homes have single-phase supply. Single-phase limits the charger to 7.4 kW maximum. Three-phase supply allows 22 kW charging for vehicles that support three-phase onboard charging. Most current electric cars in the UK accept 7.4 kW AC maximum on the onboard charger no matter whether the supply is single or three-phase. Check the car's AC charging capability before specifying a three-phase unit.
Consumer unit capacity: a 7.4 kW charger draws 32 A. The main fuse must be at least 80 A and there must be a spare way in the consumer unit for a dedicated circuit breaker.

Protective earth: most EV charge points require a TT earthing system because the DC offset from the charging circuit can blind a standard RCD. The installer fits an earth rod and connects it to the charger via a green/yellow conductor.
Smart charging capability: the unit must meet the EV Smart Charging Standard and be capable of remote scheduling. OZEV-approved installations require smart functionality.

Ask the installer for the BS 7671 test certificate and the earth electrode resistance reading. A protective earth resistance above 200 ohms requires extra electrodes. If you have solar panels. A charger with solar divert functionality can use surplus export power to charge the car rather than export it to the grid for less per kWh than you pay to import. Check this against the charger specification before purchase.

attrs.symptom: Charger trips the consumer unit RCD when charging starts

content.text: The charger draws DC residual current that is tripping the standard 30 mA RCD. The charger requires a Type B RCD rather than the standard Type A or AC. The installer should fit a Type B RCD on the dedicated charger circuit.
